{"id": "79:37/q06", "question": "How is the written final alif of 'ṭaghā' read in Warsh's cited routes?", "turns_on": "The Warsh transmission route and the treatment of a non-final form written with yāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "79:37/q06/p1", "position": "Al-Azraq's Warsh routes through Ibn Ghalbūn and others open the vowel in this non-final form.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī lists this word among the applicable non-final forms."}, {"id": "79:37/q06/p2", "position": "The al-Taysīr and related routes pronounce it between opening and imāla.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī explains this treatment by the word's being written with yāʾ."}]}
{"id": "79:37/q07", "question": "Is 'fa-ammā man ṭaghā' counted as an āya ending?", "turns_on": "The regional verse-counting tradition.", "positions": [{"id": "79:37/q07/p1", "position": "The Basran, Syrian, and Kufan counters count it as an āya ending.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī reports these regional verse counts."}, {"id": "79:37/q07/p2", "position": "The two Medinan counters and the Meccan counter do not count it as an āya ending.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī reports these regional verse counts."}]}
{"id": "79:37/q08", "question": "Why do some people prefer the immediate worldly life?", "turns_on": "The motive or orientation assigned to preference for worldly life.", "positions": [{"id": "79:37/q08/p1", "position": "Leaders recognize the Messenger's truth but resent following someone else and losing authority.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives this motive for leaders' worldly preference."}, {"id": "79:37/q08/p2", "position": "They live for the immediate moment and overlook the passing world's limits.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu says this is their usual orientation."}, {"id": "79:37/q08/p3", "position": "They favor sensory pleasure over real life.", "reasons": "Qāshānī links that preference to falling from balanced human nature into animal or predatory ranks."}]}
{"id": "79:37/q09", "question": "How does this passage divide people, and why introduce the wretched first?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:37/q09/p1", "position": "It divides people into those destined for Hell and those destined for salvation or bliss, introducing the wretched first.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the division follows the general description of Resurrection and applies to morally responsible people. {"id": "79:37/q10", "question": "What fate follows the transgression and worldly preference described here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:37/q10/p1", "position": "Hell becomes the transgressor's abode or refuge.", "reasons": "Baghawī and Ṭabrisī state the consequence. {"id": "79:37/q11", "question": "What follows for a sinner who lacks the two traits defining Hell's people?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:37/q11/p1", "position": "Such a sinner is not described as having Hell for a permanent abode.", "reasons": "Rāzī infers this from the paired conditions of transgression and preferring worldly life; Study Quran reports his explanation that their combined intellectual and practical corruption merits eternal punishment."}]}
{"id": "79:37/q12", "question": "How do fear of God and restraint of desire contrast with rebellion and worldly preference?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:37/q12/p1", "position": "Fear reflects knowledge of God and leads to obedience, while restraining caprice counters preference for worldly life.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports Rāzī's contrast: rebellion implies ignorance but fear of standing before God implies knowledge, with 35:28 cited. Ibn ʿĀshūr uses the contrast with fearing one's Lord's station in 79:40 to identify transgression as disobeying God's command. Ṭabāṭabāʾī uses fear and restraint to define the saved class against transgression and worldly preference."}]}
{"id": "79:37/q13", "question": "What does the inward reading say separates a person from ignorance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:37/q13/p1", "position": "Only one who prefers God over self, spirit, this world, and the afterlife escapes ignorance.", "reasons": "Tustarī gives this comprehensive spiritual criterion."}]}
{"id": "79:37/q14", "question": "What warnings are transmitted about preferring this world over the next?", "turns_on": "The reports give distinct warnings and consequences for the same preference.", "positions": [{"id": "79:37/q14/p1", "position": "Hudhayfa feared that this community would choose what it sees over what it knows.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports this through Juwaybir from al-Ḍaḥḥāk."}, {"id": "79:37/q14/p2", "position": "An earlier-book report says God burdens the worldly-preferring servant with worry and loss and leaves the servant to perish.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī attributes this warning to a report found in earlier books."}]}
{"id": "79:37/q15", "question": "How does this passage serve the sūra's purpose?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:37/q15/p1", "position": "It displays humanity's final fate within the sūra's proof of resurrection and gathering.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says earlier sūras had treated the matter fully and this sūra's oaths show it reaching a decisive climax."}]}
{"id": "79:37/q16", "question": "What earlier Qur'anic description is linked to the account of final fates?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:37/q16/p1", "position": "The preceding mention of people who do not hear even Hell's faintest sound connects to al-Anbiyāʾ 21:102.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī explicitly draws this link."}]}
{"id": "79:38/q01", "question": "What does āthara mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:38/q01/p1", "position": "To prefer or choose one thing over another, here worldly life over the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says īthār applies when the conditions of both choices cannot be combined. {"id": "79:38/q02", "question": "What does the root of āthara evoke here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:38/q02/p1", "position": "It evokes a remaining trace or legacy, suggesting what a person chooses to retain or leave behind.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says athar is a lasting sign, an effect is a durable trace, and āthār are remains of earlier people. {"id": "79:38/q21", "question": "How are Qurʾānic verse endings related to sajʿ and meaning?", "turns_on": "Whether sajʿ applies to the Qurʾān, whether verse endings differ from it, and whether sound may control wording or meaning.", "positions": [{"id": "79:38/q21/p1", "position": "The Qurʾān has no sajʿ.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports that some Islamic theological schools denied sajʿ categorically."}, {"id": "79:38/q21/p2", "position": "Sajʿ occurs in the Qurʾān and is part of its miraculous expression.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports that other theological schools affirmed this; most rhetoricians find no real difference between sajʿ and verse endings and explain the terminological distinction as reluctance to use a word associated with soothsayers."}, {"id": "79:38/q21/p3", "position": "Qurʾānic sajʿ is sought for its own sake and can alter order or word choice for matching endings.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ attributes this view to al-Farrāʾ."}, {"id": "79:38/q21/p4", "position": "The meanings of Qurʾānic verse endings are not subordinate to their wording.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports this denial from Ibn Sinān al-Khafājī and Ibn al-Athīr."}, {"id": "79:38/q21/p5", "position": "Qurʾānic verse endings are distinct from sajʿ.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ attributes the distinction to al-Bāqillānī and al-Rummānī; most rhetoricians regard it as a terminological reluctance tied to soothsayers."}]}

{"id": "79:39/q04", "question": "How is the possessor of al-ma'wa understood grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether al- substitutes for possession, an omitted lahu supplies the subject-predicate link, or contextual definiteness alone expresses the known possessor; Abu Hayyan and Samin dispute whether Zamakhshari's wording supplies that link.", "positions": [{"id": "79:39/q04/p1", "position": "The definite article replaces the possessive pronoun: it is his abode.", "reasons": "Zajjaj reports this and adduces the poet's 'lower the gaze,' addressed to a man whose own gaze is meant; the comparison applies to both Hell and Paradise. Nahhas, Nasafi, Samin, Burhan, Biqai, Abu Hayyan, and Alusi attribute the substitution to Kufans. Qurtubi and Baydawi state it as their analysis. Burhan connects it to Hell for one preferring worldly life and Paradise for the God-fearing. Samin cites a poem combining al- and a possessive pronoun against substitution. Alusi says the possessor is obvious and omission suits the verse-ending rhyme."}, {"id": "79:39/q04/p2", "position": "A possessive link is omitted after 'the abode': it is the abode for him.", "reasons": "Nahhas, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Burhan, Biqai, Alusi, and Tabatabai give the Basran construction al-ma'wa lahu; Razi supplies lahu because the referent is clear, comparing 'lower your gaze.' Samin says a subject-predicate link must be supplied, though omission is eased at a verse ending. He answers the Shaykh that Zamakhshari's contextual understanding amounts precisely to this Basran ellipsis. {"id": "79:39/q06", "question": "What other uses of lam are distinguished in discussion of the article?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:39/q06/p1", "position": "The article's lam is normally light; other lam forms can mark reverence, distance, affirmation, exclusivity, or emphasis.", "reasons": "Burhan says the article's lam is normally light, but in Allah it is emphatic after preceding fatha or damma to convey reverence. {"id": "79:40/q05", "question": "What does restraining the self from desire require?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:40/q05/p1", "position": "Keeping the self from forbidden acts and desires, through obedience, patience, and discipline.", "reasons": "Tabari joins obligations and avoiding sins to disliked desires; Wahidi adds desires once followed before Islam.
